item.title: A Roundtable in Celebration of Emily Lim Rogers’ Sick Work: Care Beyond the Family — Fri Nov 13, 10:00 AM — Friedl 225
item.description:
A Roundtable in Celebration of Emily Lim Rogers' Sick Work: Care Beyond the Family
Friday, November 13 New time: 10:00 - 11:00AM Friedl 216
In Sick Work (Duke University Press, Sept 2026), Emily Lim Rogers examines the everyday labor it takes to be chronically ill via an ethnographic and historical investigation of chronic fatigue syndrome. On the occasion of its publication, this roundtable features two short talks followed by a discussion, highlighting the overlaps between disability, chronic illness, kin, and care.
Zoe Wool will discuss her work on "significant otherness"-the relations of the nuclear family, and how it shows up as a US military investment in spouses as the solution to the problem of military violence that marks war veterans and renders other relations "insignificant." Anne Allison will discuss the phenomenon of kin substitution in Japan, exemplified by the rising category of "people without anyone else" and the emerging market of "rental moms" and "rental dads."

Workshop: Marx with Morgan: Toward Another Theory and History of the Commune
Friday, November 13, 2026 11:00am - 12:30pm Friedl Building, Room 107
In this workshop, Bruno Bosteels will revisit the late Marx's Ethnological Notebooks, especially his annotations of Lewis H. Morgan's Ancient Society, as an entry point into an alternative history of the Commune, much older than and distinct from the heroically defeated Paris Commune.
Bruno Bosteels is Dean of Humanities and Jesse and George Siegel Professor in the Humanities in the Department of Latin American and Iberian Cultures, with a joint appointment in the Institute for Comparative Literature and Society, at Columbia University.

item.title: Playground Economics — Fri Nov 13, 11:00 AM — None
item.description: When we think of economics, what first pops into mind might be interest rates, market indices, or mathematical formulas. Children probably wouldn't make the list. Fundamentally, though, economics concerns the consumption, production, and transfer of resources. Through this lens, children function as strategic economic decision-makers from their earliest years. I will present work exploring how children reason about and interact with resources both in individual as well as social contexts. In part one, I will discuss research revealing that children reason flexibly about the value of resources. In part two, I will focus on studies showing that children make strategic decisions about when and how many resources to transfer to others in dyadic and small groups contexts. In part three, I will review studies demonstrating that children's behavior is shaped by high-level economic factors, including norms and institutions. item.title: Environmental Justice for Environmental Science: The Challenges and Rewards of Community-Centered Research in a Time of Global Change — Fri Nov 13, 12:00 PM — None
item.description: Earth and environmental scientists sometimes think about our research as supporting efforts to promote environmental justice (i.e., environmental science for environmental justice). This framing is often true and can yield impactful science, but scientists can also benefit from flipping this perspective to consider how concepts and principles of environmental justice might sharpen our work as researchers (i.e., environmental justice for environmental science). This talk focuses on the idea that scientific research can be informed, strengthened, and even transformed through meaningful integration of environmental justice concepts, principles, and practices. I bring these ideas to life via examples from long-term partnerships with Indigenous communities in North Carolina. These partnerships aim to identify and address the impacts of industrial livestock production, fossil fuel infrastructure, and climate change on culturally significant landscapes and waterways. item.title: Pressing Prompts Community Conversation (Online) — Fri Nov 13, 12:00 PM — Virtual
item.description:
Incubated at Duke, Pressing Prompts (pressingprompts.org) is an open education resource for instructors across all disciplines who are seeking ways to integrate AI ethics into their classrooms. Unlike a static set of "best practices," Pressing Prompts is grounded in principles of critical pedagogy and educational experimentation, encouraging instructors and students to examine how AI raises crucial questions about our academic responsibilities, knowledge, labor, judgment, and learning.
In this community conversation, we will spend time hearing from faculty who have experimented with Pressing Prompts in their classrooms, answer questions and brainstorm together about how you might integrate the resource into your pedagogy, and learn from faculty about interest in and ideas for iterating Pressing Prompts for future use.

item.title: Ethnomusicology Lecture: Jessica Baker, University of Chicago — Fri Nov 13, 4:00 PM — Biddle Music Building
item.description:
Speed Meets Speed: IShowSpeed's Musical Encounters in the Caribbean
In spring 2026, Darren Watkins, the 21-year-old streamer known as IShowSpeed, livestreamed his way through fifteen Caribbean countries in under a month, backflipping, racing, eating, and musicking at the pace of a speedrun, the gaming genre built on completing a game as quickly as possible. In Island Time (2024), I argued that in the small-island Eastern Caribbean, speed is how change registers, as a felt shock. Watkins, whose brand is that he never tires, offered the region a mirror of its own speedy aesthetics, while locals in the chat and on the road commented and guided in real time. For all the polish of the corporate-sponsored tour, some encounters felt more frictional than others, often because of mishearings on both sides of the camera. item.title: Latinx Art Works: Making, Collecting, and Exhibiting America — Fri Nov 13, 4:00 PM — Smith Warehouse
item.description:
Despite making up nearly 20% of the US population, Latinx communities and their artistic contributions remain narrowly understood and severely understudied. Rather than focusing solely on matters of representation, this lecture considers what Latinx art can reveal about the United States itself: its histories of migration and belonging, race and identity, labor and cultural production, language, and the shifting boundaries of who and what constitutes "American." Drawing on her curatorial experience at the Whitney Museum of American Art and other institutions, Dr. Marcela Guerrero, DeMartini Family Curator, will examine how museums have shaped the ways Latinx art is exhibited, collected, and situated within broader narratives of American art.

item.title: The Ethics of Now with Lewis Akenji — Fri Nov 13, 7:00 PM — Durham County Library
item.description:
Join the Kenan Institute for Ethics and host Adriane Lentz-Smith for a conversation with Lewis Akenji on reorienting the economy to fight climate change and promote human well-being.
Whether pushing environments to new extremes, fracturing local economies, or heightening social tensions, climate change is impacting us all - but the way we talk about it is not leading us towards solutions. Lewis Akenji says we tend to focus on consumerist lifestyles rather than the economic structures that drive these behaviors in the first place - and the kind of society we want to build instead.
Join Akenji to explore how we can regain our agency around climate change by acting as collectives instead of individuals, and how, as communities and governments, we can address the interlinked crises of climate change and economic insecurity in ways that promote human well-being.

item.title: 250th Anniversary Celebration of Statia Day — Mon Nov 16, 1:00 PM — Union Point Park
item.description:
On 13 October 1775, the Continental Congress authorized the purchase of the merchant brigantine Defiance. The ship was acquired in mid-November and moored in Wharton and Humphreys shipyard in Philadelphia where she was converted into a warship through hull strengthening, re-rigging, and ordnance and provisioning at a cost of 300-pound sterling. She was named Andrew Doria after the 16th-century Genoese admiral Andrea Doria.
The Andrew Doria was a 14-gun Brigantine of the Continental Navy. She is most famous for her participation in the Battle of Nassau—the first amphibious engagement by the Continental Navy and the Continental Marines—and for being the first United States vessel to receive a salute from a foreign power.

item.title: Project RESTORE Educator Trek: Waterdog Warriors — Sat Dec 5, 9:00 AM — North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
item.description:
Date: Saturday, December 5, 2026. Please also mark your calendar for a rain date on Sunday, December 6! Times: 9am to 5pm
Join us in the search for one of North Carolina’s rarest salamanders, the federally threatened Neuse River waterdog, found only in the Neuse and Tar-Pamlico River Basins in North Carolina. Learn from expert biologists, explore the natural history of the waterdog, observe historically collected specimens and participate in field monitoring of the species. Discover how you can bring the excitement of field research of this rare species into your classroom.
With support from the US Fish and Wildlife Service, Project RESTORE (Rescuing Endangered Species Through Outreach, Restoration, and Education) will feature a suite of educational opportunities for teachers and students to participate in restoration and monitoring of imperiled and endangered species in eastern North Carolina.

item.title: Sold Out: Educator Trek: Great Coharie River Paddling Tour — Wed Dec 9, 8:30 AM — Depart from North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
item.description:
Calling all water-loving educators!!!
Join the NC Museum of Natural Sciences this November to explore North Carolina’s beautiful Coharie River. We will learn about the Riverkeepers restoration initiatives and hear directly from members of the Coharie Tribe about their experiences living along the river. Become familiar with one of North Carolina’s wild areas and connect with the long history of the people who call this land home.
This is an day-long event on Wednesday, December 9th. Cost: $75 (this includes the kayak rental and lunch). Participants will ride with the group from Raleigh departing at 8:30am. Transportation will be in Museum vans or bus.
Read more and register HERE! If registration is full, be sure to join the waiting list.
The full workshop fee is due when you register and payment is via credit card. Registration for most Educator Treks is on a first-come, first-served basis. Treks fill quickly, so register early!

item.title: Strengthening Families Protective Factors Training — Tue Dec 15, 9:00 AM — Virtual
item.description: Join the Positive Childhood Alliance NC on Tuesday, December 15th for a virtual introduction to the Protective Factors training. Protective factors are attributes that serve as buffers, helping parents find resources, supports, or coping strategies that allow them to parent effectively, even under stress. This course from Positive Childhood Alliance North Carolina helps child welfare systems, early education, prevention organizations, and other programs work with parents to build five protective factors that, when present, increase the overall well-being of children and families. The Five Protective Factors are the foundation to: Enhancing parental resilience, providing an array of social connections, providing parents with concrete support, helping facilitate knowledge of parenting and child development, and supporting healthy social & emotional development in young children.
